data: First Almaz military station — depressurised on orbit before any crew arrived; reentered 1973-05-28 after 54 days

The first of the three Soviet military Almaz space stations — publicly called Salyut 2 to disguise its real purpose (DoD-style reconnaissance, with a 6.4-m focal-length panoramic camera and a film-return capsule). Launched 1973-04-03 on a Proton-K from Baikonur, Salyut 2 reached orbit successfully but debris from the Proton's spent third stage — which exploded three days after launch — struck the station ~10 days later, tearing off both solar panels and puncturing the hull. The resulting power loss caused depressurisation on the 13th day (1973-04-14), rendering the station unusable before any crew could be sent. The planned crew (Pavel Popovich + Yury Artyukhin) instead flew on Salyut 3 the following year. Salyut 2 reentered the atmosphere 1973-05-28 — the shortest-lived station program in history at that point. Its existence as a military station was only declassified after the Soviet Union's collapse.

Salyut 2 was not really a Salyut at all — it was the first Almaz, a secret military reconnaissance station flown under the civilian name to hide its purpose. It never carried a crew. Days after reaching orbit it lost pressure and began to tumble, its systems failing, and it re-entered without ever being occupied. A rough, hidden start to the military half of the programme, and a reminder of how unforgiving the early station-building years were.
Second Almaz military station — Soyuz 14 crew Jul 1974; Soyuz 15 failed automatic docking; reportedly tested an onboard cannon 1975-01-24
Civilian DOS-4 station — hosted Soyuz 17 (29 days) + Soyuz 18 (63 days, then-longest spaceflight) crews; deorbited 1977-02-03
Last Almaz military station — Soyuz 21 + Soyuz 24 crews; Soyuz 23 failed approach; reentered 1977-08-08 after 412 days
